narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 68.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess risk, your application was rejected.

The strongest factor in this decision was your class ranking at the end of your third year of law school. You placed in the bottom decile, far below the average of accepted students. This single piece of information pushed the prediction heavily toward failure. Your first-year ranking also worked against you, though less strongly; you again landed in the bottom decile while accepted students averaged around the sixth.

Surprisingly, your LSAT score of 41 worked in your favor. It sits noticeably above the average of 37 for accepted applicants and pulled the prediction toward passing. However, this positive signal was not large enough to overcome the two weak academic rankings.

Your strong undergraduate GPA of 3.7, lower-middle family income, and plan to attend full-time were considered but had far less influence on the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your class standing in the remaining law-school years. A markedly better ranking in the upper half of your class would likely change the model’s prediction and open future opportunities. Consider speaking with your academic advisor about targeted support that can lift your performance before the next bar cycle.
